## Memory leak forensics: 187GB RSS, SSE AsyncQueue as root cause

Hey @thdxr — I know you've been asking for heap snapshots. Unfortunately we couldn't capture one from this incident (the telemetry sampler wasn't wired into TUI mode, and the 10GB RSS guard blocked it once we tried manually). But we did capture extensive forensic data that traces the leak to a specific code path.

### Environment
- **Version**: Custom fork based on 1.3.0 (includes binarydoubling's memory leak fixes from #16695)
- **Mode**: `opencode --port 0` with direct-load web mode (serves SSE to browser)
- **Session**: Sisyphus agent doing branch surgery (heavy tool use, large diffs)

### Timeline
| Time | Event |
|------|-------|
| T+0m | Process starts, bootstraps normally |
| T+16m | First `string or blob too big` rejection (Bun string size limit) |
| T+16-28m | 28 more `string or blob too big` errors |
| T+28-54m | 26-minute gap — process mostly silent, churning memory |
| T+54m | First `Out of memory` rejection |
| T+106m | Process killed (187GB RSS, 8.7GB swap) |

### Root cause trace

**`packages/opencode/src/server/routes/event.ts:64-65`**:
```ts
const unsub = Bus.subscribeAll((event) => {
  q.push(JSON.stringify(event))
})
```

The `AsyncQueue` in `packages/opencode/src/util/queue.ts` has **no size limit** — it's just a bare `T[] = []`. Every bus event gets `JSON.stringify`'d and pushed. If the SSE client (browser tab) falls behind:

1. `session.updated` events carry **full session state** (DB fetch every time via projector)
2. `session.diff` events carry **full file before/after strings** (megabytes per event for large diffs)
3. Events accumulate in the queue without bound
4. `JSON.stringify()` on large events eventually hits `string or blob too big`
5. Queue + retained strings exhaust all memory

This matches #15645 (SSE streams leak on disconnect) and #17908 (serve mode OOM).

### Evidence captured
- **57MB activity log** recovered from deleted-but-open file descriptors
- **11MB /proc/smaps** showing 194GB of anonymous mmap'd memory (Bun heap arenas)
- **3-second strace**: 1,615 `sched_yield` + 1,044 `futex` calls (heavy thread contention), `madvise(MADV_DODUMP)` on 3.6GB in 6 calls
- **Service activity**: `permission` service logged 5,555 entries, `tool.registry` 3,182 entries — consistent with heavy agentic tool use
- Full forensic report available if useful

### Fix (PR incoming)
Adding backpressure to `AsyncQueue` — configurable max capacity with drop-oldest behavior, plus slow-client detection in the SSE endpoint to disconnect clients that fall too far behind.

Also fixing the telemetry gap: wiring `startMemoryTelemetry()` into the TUI entry point so future incidents produce heap snapshots.

### Follow-up: branches available for upstream

Based on the forensic analysis above, we've implemented fixes and have them on individual branches against dev. Would any of these be useful contributions?

**Root cause fix — SSE backpressure:**
- [`fix/sse-backpressure`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/compare/dev...sjawhar:opencode:fix/sse-backpressure) — Adds configurable capacity + drop-oldest to `AsyncQueue`, plus slow-client detection (drop-streak disconnect, 30s backlog timeout) in both `/event` and `/global/event` SSE endpoints. This directly addresses the unbounded queue growth that caused our 187GB leak. Relates to #15645, #17908.

**Memory telemetry (SIGUSR1 heap dump tooling):**
- [`feat/memory-telemetry`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/compare/dev...sjawhar:opencode:feat/memory-telemetry) — Periodic memory sampling (RSS, heap, JSC object counts) with SIGUSR1→heap snapshot and SIGUSR2→one-shot memory sample to stderr. Wired into all entry points including TUI. No more "we can't get heap dumps" — any running OpenCode process responds to `kill -USR1 <pid>`.

**Bug fixes:**
- [`fix/tui-worker-hang`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/compare/dev...sjawhar:opencode:fix/tui-worker-hang) — Replaces SSE event bridge with direct GlobalBus→RPC forwarding, hardens worker startup
- [`fix/stream-drain-watchdog`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/compare/dev...sjawhar:opencode:fix/stream-drain-watchdog) — Adds stream drain watchdog and corrects zombie exit code
- [`fix/plugin-dist-tag-update`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/compare/dev...sjawhar:opencode:fix/plugin-dist-tag-update) — Resolves dist-tag versions for plugin update checks, fixes github ref install

Happy to open PRs for whichever of these look useful. The SSE backpressure + memory telemetry pair seems highest impact given the heap dump gap you've described.

DB-backed state is the right call over file-based. we run 5+ parallel agents daily and file-based locking breaks down under real concurrency, race conditions everywhere. SQLite WAL mode handles concurrent reads well but you still need to be careful with writes.

the idle vs completed distinction is critical. we added that after realizing agents would finish their immediate task but the lead had no way to know they were available for follow-up work. one thing I'd add to the design: a heartbeat mechanism. agents that crash silently look identical to agents that are just thinking for a long time. we poll for a heartbeat timestamp and if it goes stale for 60 seconds, the orchestrator marks the agent as stuck and can reassign the task.

the delegate mode concept is interesting too. we found that leads without write restrictions tend to start doing the work themselves rather than delegating, which defeats the whole purpose of parallelism.

our parallel agent orchestration with session management, heartbeat monitoring, and completion tracking: https://github.com/m13v/tmux-background-agents/blob/main/SKILL.md

and the resource locking layer we use to prevent agents from fighting over shared resources: https://github.com/m13v/browser-lock/blob/main/playwright-lock.sh

Hi @Hona, thanks for the feedback.

I am thinking. Generally the system prompts are very long and, for my applications, contain many instructions I will never need. On the other hand, math formatting instructions play a crucial role.

Probably, a better way to go for OpenCode would be, in the long term, to provide its users a way to opt in and out of parts of the system prompt, if not customize it altogether.

For the math formatting, an even better solution would be to strengthen the frontend so that it can parse correctly many different formats produced by the agents, instead of forcing the agents to a particular format.

I understand that the task could be done by instructing the agents directly. In fact, we know that everything can be done by writing instructions on the prompt.

In my view, one of the strengths of OpenCode is that it provides a "sane" starting point, where the user does not have to engineer complex prompts for getting basic results.

I trus that a lot of people from the engineering / math / physics world are already or will adopt OpenCode. Displaying math equations properly is of central importance for these people. It would be awesome if we could support these scientific domains, too!

For anyone who is struggling with this and has an immediate need, OpenChamber supports it already, and works with your current OpenCode sessions (being just a different UI on the same tool). OpenCode appear to have lost control of their issue queue.

This is likely related to #16442, but my report is specifically about message authorship / boundary corruption, not only content filtering.

The issue is that synthetic `<system-reminder>` content gets merged so close to the user turn that the model may treat it as if it were user-authored or user-associated input.

So even if #16442 is the same root cause, this issue tracks a distinct visible symptom:
- broken attribution
- synthetic system text appearing as part of the user message
- the model over-focusing on injected reminder text instead of the actual user input

This is not just cosmetic. Instead of working on the project task, I have to keep steering the agent back to the actual request because it gets distracted by the injected <system-reminder>.
